class="q">Control</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">By design hawk and eagle decide threads, launches and scheduling, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches; for hand-tuned class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="deploy"><th scope="row" class="q">Deploy</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Kernels run inside Python; modules can be compiled ahead of time but need the Warp runtime.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="extensible"><th scope="row" class="q">Extensibility</th><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two backends today (CUDA and CPU threads), no second vendor yet.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">NVIDIA GPUs and the CPU; no public path to add a backend.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.</small></td></tr></tbody></table></details></div>

class="ok">22 lines (1.0× the best) ✓</td></tr><tr data-feature="tensor"><th scope="row" class="q">Tensors</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Built for per-sample kernels and ensembles; for dense tensor work it hands arrays to PyTorch or JAX zero-copy.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Per-thread kernels are its home ground; it also offers matrix and tile types for dense blocks.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Array programs written once and compiled by XLA; batched linear algebra, convolutions and broadcasting are first-class.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Dense array maths is its home ground, with tuned libraries behind batched linear algebra, convolutions and broadcasting.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="array_style"><th scope="row" class="q">Array style</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">A per-sample kernel language by design: you write one step of one sample, and whole-array code is left to array libraries, with which raptor exchanges arrays zero-copy.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">You write per-thread kernels; whole-array expressions are not the model.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">NumPy-style array expressions, but functional and traced rather than eager.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Eager tensor expressions are the programming model.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="half_precision"><th scope="row" class="q">Half precision</th><td class="no">1 of 5<br><small class="why">Not supported. raptor is scoped to FP32 and FP64 numerics; half-precision and tensor-core work belongs with PyTorch or JAX.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">float16 support and tile operations that can use tensor cores.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">FP16, BF16 and FP8 types, with XLA targeting tensor cores.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">FP16, BF16 and FP8 types with tensor-core paths, including autocast.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="single_thread"><th scope="row" class="q">Single-thread</th><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">You write one step of one sample; hawk and eagle handle threads, launches, stopping and compaction.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A per-thread kernel: you index and loop yourself, and choose the launch.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A per-sample function under vmap; early stopping becomes masking you write.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">torch.func.vmap over a per-sample function; stopping and batching stay with you.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="differentiable"><th scope="row" class="q">Derivatives</th><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Every kernel written in hawk&#x27;s own vocabulary carries generated forward- and reverse-mode derivatives, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Reverse mode through wp.Tape over its kernels, with its emphasis on reverse mode over the tape.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Forward and reverse mode through grad, jvp and vjp, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Autograd differentiates tensor programs; a custom kernel needs its backward written by hand.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="control"><th scope="row" class="q">Control</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">By design hawk and eagle decide threads, launches and scheduling, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches; for hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">You write the per-thread kernel and choose its launch: near-total control short of raw CUDA, the right choice for hand-tuned kernels.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Pallas exposes kernel-level control; plain JAX leaves scheduling to XLA.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="arrays"><th scope="row" class="q">Your arrays</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp and NumPy today, not JAX).</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy views of PyTorch, JAX and NumPy arrays.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="deploy"><th scope="row" class="q">Deploy</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Kernels run inside Python; modules can be compiled ahead of time but need the Warp runtime.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="extensible"><th scope="row" class="q">Extensibility</th><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two backends today (CUDA and CPU threads), no second vendor yet.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">NVIDIA GPUs and the CPU; no public path to add a backend.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.</small></td></tr></tbody></table></details></div>

kernels; whole-array expressions are not the model.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">NumPy-style array expressions, but functional and traced rather than class="why">A per-sample function under vmap; early stopping becomes masking you write.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">torch.func.vmap over a per-sample function; stopping and batching stay with you.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="differentiable"><th scope="row" class="q">Derivatives</th><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Every kernel written in hawk&#x27;s own vocabulary carries generated forward- and reverse-mode derivatives, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Reverse mode through wp.Tape over its kernels, with its emphasis on reverse mode over the tape.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Forward and reverse mode through grad, jvp and vjp, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Autograd differentiates tensor programs; a custom kernel needs its backward written by hand.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="control"><th scope="row" class="q">Control</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">By design hawk and eagle decide threads, launches and scheduling, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches; for hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">You write the per-thread kernel and choose its launch: near-total control short of raw CUDA, the right choice for hand-tuned kernels.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Pallas exposes kernel-level control; plain JAX leaves scheduling to XLA.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="arrays"><th scope="row" class="q">Your arrays</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp and NumPy today, not JAX).</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy views of PyTorch, JAX and NumPy arrays.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="deploy"><th scope="row" class="q">Deploy</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Kernels run inside Python; modules can be compiled ahead of time but need the Warp runtime.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="extensible"><th scope="row" class="q">Extensibility</th><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two backends today (CUDA and CPU threads), no second vendor yet.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">NVIDIA GPUs and the CPU; no public path to add a backend.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.</small></td></tr></tbody></table></details></div>

precision</th><td class="no">1 of 5<br><small class="why">Not supported. raptor is scoped to FP32 and FP64 numerics; half-precision and tensor-core work belongs with PyTorch or JAX.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">float16 support and tile operations that can use tensor cores.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">FP16, BF16 and FP8 types, with XLA targeting tensor cores.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">FP16, BF16 and FP8 types with tensor-core paths, including autocast.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="single_thread"><th scope="row" class="q">Single-thread</th><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">You write one step of one sample; hawk and eagle handle threads, launches, stopping and compaction.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A per-thread kernel: you index and loop yourself, and choose the launch.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A per-sample function under vmap; early stopping becomes masking you write.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">torch.func.vmap over a per-sample function; stopping and batching stay with you.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="differentiable"><th scope="row" class="q">Derivatives</th><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Every kernel written in hawk&#x27;s own vocabulary carries generated forward- and reverse-mode derivatives, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Reverse mode through wp.Tape over its kernels, with its emphasis on reverse mode over the tape.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Forward and reverse mode through grad, jvp and vjp, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Autograd differentiates tensor programs; a custom kernel needs its backward written by hand.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="control"><th scope="row" class="q">Control</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">By design hawk and eagle decide threads, launches and scheduling, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches; for hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">You write the per-thread kernel and choose its launch: near-total control short of raw CUDA, the right choice for hand-tuned kernels.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Pallas exposes kernel-level control; plain JAX leaves scheduling to XLA.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="arrays"><th scope="row" class="q">Your arrays</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp and NumPy today, not JAX).</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy views of PyTorch, JAX and NumPy arrays.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="deploy"><th scope="row" class="q">Deploy</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Kernels run inside Python; modules can be compiled ahead of time but need the Warp runtime.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="extensible"><th scope="row" class="q">Extensibility</th><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two backends today (CUDA and CPU threads), no second vendor yet.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">NVIDIA GPUs and the CPU; no public path to add a backend.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.</small></td></tr></tbody></table></details></div>

to PyTorch or JAX zero-copy.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Per-thread kernels are its home ground; it also offers matrix and tile types for dense blocks.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Array programs written once and compiled by XLA; batched linear algebra, convolutions and broadcasting are first-class.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Dense array maths is its home ground, with tuned libraries behind batched linear algebra, convolutions and broadcasting.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="array_style"><th scope="row" class="q">Array style</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">A per-sample kernel language by design: you write one step of one sample, and whole-array code is left to array libraries, with which raptor exchanges arrays zero-copy.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">You write per-thread kernels; whole-array expressions are not the model.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">NumPy-style array expressions, but functional and traced rather than eager.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Eager tensor expressions are the programming model.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="half_precision"><th scope="row" class="q">Half precision</th><td class="no">1 of 5<br><small support and tile operations that can use tensor cores.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">FP16, BF16 and FP8 types, with XLA targeting tensor cores.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">FP16, BF16 and FP8 types with tensor-core paths, including autocast.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="single_thread"><th scope="row" class="q">Single-thread</th><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">You write one step of one sample; hawk and eagle handle threads, launches, stopping and compaction.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A per-thread kernel: you index and loop yourself, and choose the launch.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A per-sample function under vmap; early stopping becomes masking you write.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">torch.func.vmap over a per-sample function; stopping and batching stay with you.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="differentiable"><th scope="row" class="q">Derivatives</th><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Every kernel written in hawk&#x27;s own vocabulary carries generated forward- and reverse-mode derivatives, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Reverse mode through wp.Tape over its kernels, with its emphasis on reverse mode over the tape.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Forward and reverse mode through grad, jvp and vjp, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Autograd differentiates tensor programs; a custom kernel needs its backward written by hand.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="control"><th scope="row" class="q">Control</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">By design hawk and eagle decide threads, launches and scheduling, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches; for hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">You write the per-thread kernel and choose its launch: near-total control short of raw CUDA, the right choice for hand-tuned kernels.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Pallas exposes kernel-level control; plain JAX leaves scheduling to XLA.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="arrays"><th scope="row" class="q">Your arrays</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp and NumPy today, not JAX).</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy views of PyTorch, JAX and NumPy arrays.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="deploy"><th scope="row" class="q">Deploy</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Kernels run inside Python; modules can be compiled ahead of time but need the Warp runtime.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="extensible"><th scope="row" class="q">Extensibility</th><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two backends today (CUDA and CPU threads), no second vendor yet.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">NVIDIA GPUs and the CPU; no public path to add a backend.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.</small></td></tr></tbody></table></details></div>

class="why">A per-sample function under vmap; early stopping becomes masking you write.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">torch.func.vmap over a per-sample function; stopping and batching stay with you.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="differentiable"><th scope="row" class="q">Derivatives</th><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Every kernel written in hawk&#x27;s its emphasis on reverse mode over the tape.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Forward and reverse mode through grad, jvp and vjp, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Autograd differentiates tensor programs; a custom kernel needs its backward written by hand.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="control"><th scope="row" class="q">Control</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">By design hawk and eagle decide threads, launches and scheduling, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches; for hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">You write the per-thread kernel and choose its launch: near-total control short of raw CUDA, the right choice for hand-tuned kernels.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Pallas exposes kernel-level control; plain JAX leaves scheduling to XLA.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="arrays"><th scope="row" class="q">Your arrays</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp and NumPy today, not JAX).</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy views of PyTorch, JAX and NumPy arrays.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="deploy"><th scope="row" class="q">Deploy</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Kernels run inside Python; modules can be compiled ahead of time but need the Warp runtime.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="extensible"><th scope="row" class="q">Extensibility</th><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two backends today (CUDA and CPU threads), no second vendor yet.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">NVIDIA GPUs and the CPU; no public path to add a backend.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.</small></td></tr></tbody></table></details></div>

<dl class="radar-defs" aria-label="What each axis measures"><dt>Uneven ensembles</dt><dd>How long a batch takes when every sample stops at its own step, at the largest batch.</dd><dt>Regular ensembles</dt><dd>How long a batch takes when every sample runs the same number of steps, at the largest batch.</dd><dt>Small jobs</dt><dd>Wall time of the smallest batch, where launch overhead matters most.</dd><dt>Adaptive ODEs</dt><dd>Wall time of an adaptive-step orbit propagator (RK7(8)) at the largest batch.</dd><dt>Memory</dt><dd>Peak memory the process holds for the same workload (device memory on a GPU; host memory on a CPU at N = 1,000,000 only, net of the benchmark harness&#x27;s own copies).</dd><dt>Compile time</dt><dd>Cold compile of the complex adaptive kernel (RK7(8) orbits) on empty caches; the simple oscillator&#x27;s time and the growth factor are listed per tool. A tool with nothing to compile sits at the edge. Compiled once per kernel; raptor&#x27;s compile does not depend on the problem size N.</dd><dt>Code size</dt><dd>Lines of code the task takes, non-blank and non-comment.</dd><dt>Tensor workloads (qualitative)</dt><dd>Tensor workloads (qualitative): how naturally a tool expresses dense array maths (batched linear algebra, convolutions, broadcasting) and how much of it its tuned libraries cover. 5 = this is its home ground.</dd><dt>Array-style programming (qualitative)</dt><dd>Array-style programming (qualitative): how naturally you write whole-array expressions eagerly, the NumPy way. 5 = the array expression is the programming model. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Half precision and below (qualitative)</dt><dd>Half precision and below (qualitative): FP16, BF16, FP8 and FP4 arithmetic and tensor cores (FP32 and FP64 are measured on the other axes). 5 = these formats and tensor cores are first-class paths. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Single-thread abstraction (qualitative)</dt><dd>Single-thread abstraction (qualitative): how fully you can write the code for one sample, one step, and let the tool run it over the batch: threads, launches, early stopping and scheduling included. 5 = you write one sample and nothing else. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Differentiable kernels (qualitative)</dt><dd>Differentiable kernels (qualitative): how directly you get forward- and reverse-mode derivatives of your own kernels, on GPU and on CPU. 5 = built in for every kernel written in the tool&#x27;s own vocabulary.</dd><dt>Low-level control (qualitative)</dt><dd>Low-level control (qualitative): how much of the GPU&#x27;s execution you control from the tool&#x27;s own language: thread indexing, shared memory, atomics, launch shape, synchronisation (raw CUDA/C++ not counted). 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched. On a CPU the same question is asked of threads, SIMD and memory layout. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Works with your arrays (qualitative)</dt><dd>Works with your arrays (qualitative): how freely arrays move to and from other frameworks without copies. 5 = zero-copy exchange is the norm.</dd><dt>Deploy outside Python (qualitative)</dt><dd>Deploy outside Python (qualitative): whether a compiled kernel can run from programs that are not Python. 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.</dd><dt>Extensibility (qualitative)</dt><dd>Extensibility (qualitative): how readily new hardware, backends and features can be added without losing speed. 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd></dl>

<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-note-lead">Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.</p>
<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-caption-control">NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.</p>
<details class="radar-data radar-howto"><summary>How to read this radar</summary><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-majors"><li><strong>Ensemble speed</strong>: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.</li><li><strong>Footprint and turnaround</strong>: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.</li><li><strong>Tensors and precision</strong>: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.</li><li><strong>One-sample authoring</strong>: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Reach</strong>: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (compile time: fixed, 0.1 s to 100 s; code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note">Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing or, for compile time, is the tool's simple-kernel time. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-anchors"><li><strong>Tensor workloads</strong>: 5 = dense array maths, batched linear algebra and convolutions are its home ground.</li><li><strong>Array-style programming</strong>: 5 = the whole-array expression is the programming model.</li><li><strong>Half precision and below</strong>: 5 = FP16, BF16, FP8, FP4 and tensor cores are first-class paths.</li><li><strong>Single-thread abstraction</strong>: 5 = you write one sample and nothing else.</li><li><strong>Differentiable kernels</strong>: 5 = derivatives are built in for every kernel written in the tool.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched.</li><li><strong>Works with your arrays</strong>: 5 = zero-copy exchange with other frameworks is the norm.</li><li><strong>Deploy outside Python</strong>: 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.</li><li><strong>Extensibility</strong>: 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note"><a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, in the full tables</a>.</p></details>

hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">prange, explicit threads and typed loops; SIMD and memory layout are yours.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Plain JAX leaves threads, vectorisation and layout to XLA; Pallas control is aimed at the GPU.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Strides and memory layout are yours to choose; threads and SIMD are left to the libraries underneath.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="arrays"><th scope="row" class="q">Your arrays</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp and NumPy today, not JAX).</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Reads NumPy arrays directly and exposes the CUDA array interface; wider exchange takes some glue.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">The array protocols everyone reads, on the host; device memory is out of its scope.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="deploy"><th scope="row" class="q">Deploy</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Ahead-of-time compilation exists in a limited form; most use stays inside Python.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.</small></td><td class="no">1 of 5<br><small class="why">A Python library; nothing is compiled into a separate artefact.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="extensible"><th scope="row" class="q">Extensibility</th><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two backends today (CUDA and CPU threads), no second vendor yet.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">An extension API for new types and targets, at a low level.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Array-API dispatch lets other array libraries stand in.</small></td></tr></tbody></table></details></div>

of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Forward and reverse mode through grad, jvp and vjp, on GPU and CPU.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Autograd differentiates tensor programs; a scope="row" class="q">Control</th><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">By design hawk and eagle decide threads, launches and scheduling, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches; for hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.</small></td><td class="ok">5 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">prange, explicit threads and typed loops; SIMD and memory layout are yours.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Plain JAX leaves threads, vectorisation and layout to XLA; Pallas control is aimed at the GPU.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Strides and memory layout are yours to choose; threads and SIMD are left to the libraries underneath.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="arrays"><th scope="row" class="q">Your arrays</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp and NumPy today, not JAX).</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Reads NumPy arrays directly and exposes the CUDA array interface; wider exchange takes some glue.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">The array protocols everyone reads, on the host; device memory is out of its scope.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="deploy"><th scope="row" class="q">Deploy</th><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.</small></td><td class="no">2 of 5<br><small class="why">Ahead-of-time compilation exists in a limited form; most use stays inside Python.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.</small></td><td class="no">1 of 5<br><small class="why">A Python library; nothing is compiled into a separate artefact.</small></td></tr><tr data-feature="extensible"><th scope="row" class="q">Extensibility</th><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two backends today (CUDA and CPU threads), no second vendor yet.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">An extension API for new types and targets, at a low level.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.</small></td><td class="ok">4 of 5 ✓<br><small class="why">Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.</small></td><td class="no">3 of 5<br><small class="why">Array-API dispatch lets other array libraries stand in.</small></td></tr></tbody></table></details></div>

<dl class="radar-defs" aria-label="What each axis measures"><dt>Uneven ensembles</dt><dd>How long a batch takes when every sample stops at its own step, at the largest batch.</dd><dt>Regular ensembles</dt><dd>How long a batch takes when every sample runs the same number of steps, at the largest batch.</dd><dt>Small jobs</dt><dd>Wall time of the smallest batch, where launch overhead matters most.</dd><dt>Adaptive ODEs</dt><dd>Wall time of an adaptive-step orbit propagator (RK7(8)) at the largest batch.</dd><dt>Memory</dt><dd>Peak memory the process holds for the same workload (device memory on a GPU; host memory on a CPU at N = 1,000,000 only, net of the benchmark harness&#x27;s own copies).</dd><dt>Compile time</dt><dd>Cold compile of the complex adaptive kernel (RK7(8) orbits) on empty caches; the simple oscillator&#x27;s time and the growth factor are listed per tool. A tool with nothing to compile sits at the edge. Compiled once per kernel; raptor&#x27;s compile does not depend on the problem size N.</dd><dt>Code size</dt><dd>Lines of code the task takes, non-blank and non-comment.</dd><dt>Tensor workloads (qualitative)</dt><dd>Tensor workloads (qualitative): how naturally a tool expresses dense array maths (batched linear algebra, convolutions, broadcasting) and how much of it its tuned libraries cover. 5 = this is its home ground.</dd><dt>Array-style programming (qualitative)</dt><dd>Array-style programming (qualitative): how naturally you write whole-array expressions eagerly, the NumPy way. 5 = the array expression is the programming model. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Half precision and below (qualitative)</dt><dd>Half precision and below (qualitative): FP16, BF16, FP8 and FP4 arithmetic and tensor cores (FP32 and FP64 are measured on the other axes). 5 = these formats and tensor cores are first-class paths. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Single-thread abstraction (qualitative)</dt><dd>Single-thread abstraction (qualitative): how fully you can write the code for one sample, one step, and let the tool run it over the batch: threads, launches, early stopping and scheduling included. 5 = you write one sample and nothing else. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Differentiable kernels (qualitative)</dt><dd>Differentiable kernels (qualitative): how directly you get forward- and reverse-mode derivatives of your own kernels, on GPU and on CPU. 5 = built in for every kernel written in the tool&#x27;s own vocabulary.</dd><dt>Low-level control (qualitative)</dt><dd>Low-level control (qualitative): how much of the GPU&#x27;s execution you control from the tool&#x27;s own language: thread indexing, shared memory, atomics, launch shape, synchronisation (raw CUDA/C++ not counted). 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched. On a CPU the same question is asked of threads, SIMD and memory layout. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Works with your arrays (qualitative)</dt><dd>Works with your arrays (qualitative): how freely arrays move to and from other frameworks without copies. 5 = zero-copy exchange is the norm.</dd><dt>Deploy outside Python (qualitative)</dt><dd>Deploy outside Python (qualitative): whether a compiled kernel can run from programs that are not Python. 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.</dd><dt>Extensibility (qualitative)</dt><dd>Extensibility (qualitative): how readily new hardware, backends and features can be added without losing speed. 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd></dl>

<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-note-lead">Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.</p>
<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-caption-control">NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.</p>
<details class="radar-data radar-howto"><summary>How to read this radar</summary><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-majors"><li><strong>Ensemble speed</strong>: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.</li><li><strong>Footprint and turnaround</strong>: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.</li><li><strong>Tensors and precision</strong>: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.</li><li><strong>One-sample authoring</strong>: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Reach</strong>: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (compile time: fixed, 0.1 s to 100 s; code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note">Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing or, for compile time, is the tool's simple-kernel time.
